intro: Violas and cellos begin a gentle A♭-major song over plucked basses. Beethoven keeps finding new ways to dress it, while trumpets and timpani repeatedly interrupt with a C-major fanfare.

sections.label: A · Low strings sing, trumpets answer
sections.mNote: An A♭-major melody meets a C-major fanfare

sections.label: A′ · The melody fills with semiquavers
sections.mNote: Violas and cellos decorate their opening song

sections.label: A″ · Quicker notes, then woodwind solos
sections.mNote: Demisemiquavers in the low strings; clarinet, bassoon and flute follow

sections.label: B · The fanfare dwindles into minor
sections.mNote: Quieter string figures lead towards A♭ minor

cues.title: Violas and cellos sing
cues.text: The violins wait. Violas and cellos sing in octaves, with a dotted rhythm that gives the A♭-major melody a gentle swing. Underneath, the double basses pluck their notes. Beethoven marks the tune dolce, sweetly.
cues.evidence: Beethoven, Werke, Serie 1 No. 5, Breitkopf & Härtel, printed p. 22, opening of Andante con moto: viola and cello octaves, pizzicato bass and dolce. Mutopia 1437 reproduces these parts.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The trumpets answer in C
cues.text: The orchestra breaks into C major. Trumpets and timpani reinforce the dotted tune, while the strings run beneath it. The quiet song has acquired a public, ceremonial voice.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, printed p. 23: C-major statement with trumpets, timpani and running string accompaniment.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The tune grows smaller notes
cues.text: Violas and cellos recover the opening melody in A♭ major, now filling its outline with semiquavers. Plucked basses support them again. The extra notes make the tune flow without changing its three-beat bar.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 24, first variation; Mutopia 1437, viola, cello and bass parts. The metre remains 3/8.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two names on the title-page
cues.text: Prince Lobkowitz and Count Razumovsky share the Fifth’s dedication. Both names also appear on the Sixth Symphony, its companion at the 1808 première.
cues.evidence: Dedication and joint première of the Fifth and Sixth: Eastman School of Music, https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/.

cues.title: The bow works harder
cues.text: The lower strings divide the tune into still quicker notes: demisemiquavers. The melody’s outline survives inside the fast bow strokes. Later a fermata clears the air for a quieter succession of clarinet, bassoon and flute phrases.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 27–30: demisemiquaver variation, fermata and woodwind continuation. Mutopia 1437, cello part, distinguishes this return from the earlier semiquavers.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The fanfare loses its brass
cues.text: The third C-major fanfare dies down. Trumpets and timpani withdraw, leaving smaller figures in the strings and woodwind. A♭ minor darkens the familiar tune before the opening melody can return in full.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 31–33: diminuendo, reduced scoring, A♭-minor passage and following A♭-major return. The cue covers the episode beginning at the existing section boundary.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The song fills the orchestra
cues.text: The opening tune returns in A♭ major, fortissimo. Winds and violins sing the line that began in violas and cellos, while the lower strings play quick accompanying figures. The melody can bear all that weight.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 33, lower system: full A♭-major return, ff, melody in winds and first violins, rapid lower-string accompaniment.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A bassoon takes a walk
cues.text: The coda gives the bassoon a little solo above detached strings. Più moto asks for more movement, still in 3/8. A♭ remains home; Tempo I later restores the opening pace for the last phrases.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 34–35: Più moto, bassoon solo and detached strings, followed by Tempo I.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A♭ has the last word
cues.text: The final cadences bring the bass from E♭ to A♭. The key of the low strings’ opening song closes the movement, with the whole orchestra joining in.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 36: closing E♭–A♭ cadences and orchestral A♭-major ending.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The bass slips back to A♭
transitions.from: A · Low strings sing, trumpets answer
transitions.to: A′ · The melody fills with semiquavers
transitions.how: After the C-major fanfare, the bass descends E–E♭–D–D♭–C, then turns through D♭ to E♭. That last note is A♭ major’s dominant. Violas and cellos bring back the opening melody in semiquavers, above plucked basses. The brass falls silent, and the Andante continues at the same pace.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 23–24; Mutopia 1437, cello and bass parts, chromatic link and first variation.

transitions.title: A second descent, still quicker notes
transitions.from: A′ · The melody fills with semiquavers
transitions.to: A″ · Quicker notes, then woodwind solos
transitions.how: The C-major fanfare again withdraws through the bass’s E–E♭–D–D♭–C descent. The return to A♭ major brings the low-string melody in demisemiquavers. Its notes crowd together inside the same 3/8 bars, with the original tune still shaping their rise and fall.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 27–28; Mutopia 1437, cello part, second chromatic link and demisemiquaver return.

transitions.title: The brass withdraws
transitions.from: A″ · Quicker notes, then woodwind solos
transitions.to: B · The fanfare dwindles into minor
transitions.how: The C-major fanfare diminishes. Trumpets and timpani stop while the strings continue with small repeated figures, passing them between upper and lower parts. Woodwind join the quieter conversation. The following A♭-minor passage introduces C♭ and G♭ into the tune’s familiar outline.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 31–32, diminuendo and subsequent minor-mode writing; Mutopia 1437 cello part includes C♭ and G♭.

transitions.title: The full orchestra recovers the song
transitions.from: B · The fanfare dwindles into minor
transitions.to: A‴ · The whole orchestra takes the tune
transitions.how: Rising figures pass through the strings, with a crescendo drawing in the winds. The opening melody arrives fortissimo in A♭ major. Winds and first violins sing it together, while violas and cellos fill the accompaniment with quick notes above the basses’ A♭.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 33, crescendo and full A♭-major return.

transitions.title: The bassoon quickens the step
transitions.from: A‴ · The whole orchestra takes the tune
transitions.to: Coda · A bassoon quickens the step
transitions.how: The full A♭-major statement gives way to quieter strings. At Più moto, a bassoon sings above detached chords and short bass notes; the three-quaver bar remains. The wind and strings gradually build another crescendo before Tempo I restores the original pace.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 34–35: Più moto bassoon solo, detached strings, crescendo and Tempo I.

source.title: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, II, Breitkopf & Härtel full score, plate B.5
source.locator: Printed pp. 22–36; viola, cello and bass parts also in Mutopia 1437.

timeline.note: Violas and cellos sing the dotted melody above plucked double basses.
The winds answer the low strings; the violins join the conversation.
Trumpets and timpani join the C-major fanfare, with running strings beneath it.
The brass falls silent while the bass descends by semitones.
Violas and cellos decorate the melody in semiquavers beneath a held clarinet note and plucked violins.
Clarinets and bassoons answer the strings’ decorated melody.
Trumpets and timpani return for the second C-major fanfare.
The bass repeats its chromatic descent as the trumpets and timpani withdraw.
Violas and cellos play demisemiquavers under held wind notes and plucked violins.
Quick lower-string figures run beneath accented orchestral chords.
A fermata clears the way for clarinet, bassoon and flute phrases over detached strings.
The full orchestra gathers for the third C-major fanfare.
Small string figures and woodwind replies lead towards A♭ minor.
Winds and violins sing the opening tune fortissimo above quick lower strings.
A bassoon sings above detached strings at Più moto.
Tempo I restores the opening pace, with wind replies above the strings.
A crescendo draws the orchestra into the final A♭-major cadences.

composer.epithet: He could make a symphony out of four notes, and spent his last years finding things four string players had never said.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. Music was the family trade. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, learning operas from the middle of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was supposed to come back. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him disappeared.
